content:
According to Mark Gurman's latest Power On newsletter, Apple is reportedly considering several changes to its App Store. The goal? To boost potential revenue.

The specific plans Apple has for App Store changes remain unclear. Bloomberg's Mark Gurman reports that Apple wants to "find ways to improve profit margins and extract more recurring revenue from the platform," with the effort being driven primarily by incoming CEO John Ternus and current Senior Vice President of Services Eddy Cue.

The initiative is also reportedly part of the reason veteran employee Phil Schiller left the company last week. After stepping down as Senior Vice President of Marketing in 2020, Schiller took on the role of Apple Fellow, with some of his responsibilities including overseeing the App Store. Schiller reportedly had zero interest in the idea:

There are many ways Apple could improve App Store profit margins. For example, it could eliminate the existing human app review process — though in the age of automated coding, its usefulness has likely diminished significantly, the process is costly. Further automating reviews, however, may not sit well with users, even if it does help reduce costs.

Apple could also raise developer membership fees, currently $99 per year. Given that many small developers spend $200 per month on Codex and Claude subscriptions to build apps, it's easy to see why Apple might have reason to raise prices, and developers would still be willing to pay. Apple could also charge large developers subscription fees based on traffic, passing on some of the infrastructure costs.

What ultimately develops remains to be seen, but I'm very much looking forward to seeing what these changes end up looking like.
